Trading Unemployed Americans can gain financial security through options trading, according to a new report from the CBOE Options Institute. The report explains how options can help people collect unemployment insurance-like income during periods of unemployment.
The report, titled "Options as a Safety Net: A New Way to Approach Un employment Insurance," explains that options are financial instruments that give the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specified price on or before a certain date. Options trading can be used to generate income, manage risk, and even create a "virtual unemployment benefit."
Here's how it works: An unemployed person can sell, or write, a put option on a stock index, such as the S&P 500, that they believe will not decline below a specific price. In exchange for writing the option, the seller receives a premium payment. If the stock market does not fall below the specifiedprice, then the buyer of the put will let it expire worthless, leaving the premium with the options seller. However, if the marketdoes decline,the buyer can exercise theoption, forcing theseller to sell the underlying stock at the agreed-upon price, thus generating a loss for theoptions seller but providing a financial safety net for those who have lost their jobs. This strategy is similar to collecting unemployment benefits, as it provides a source of income when needed. Additionally, unlike traditional unemploymentbenefits, this strategy doesnot require the individual to have previously earned a minimum income or paid into a fund. Anyone can participate in options markets, regardless of their employment status. "The beauty of options as an alternative safetynet is that it doesnt require a pre-existing relationship between the insurer and theinsured," said Steve Sanders, CMO of Cboe Global Markets, Inc. and co-author ofthe report. He added, "All that isrequiredis a trade between two consenting adults, which can take place entirely online." The CBoEOptions Institute report also provides guidance on how to get started with optionstrading, including resources for education and training. It is important to note thatoptions trading carries risk and is not suitable for everyone. Therefore, it is recommended that those interested in using options for income supplementation during unemployment consult with a qualified financial professional before getting started. In your case, if you sell some investments that have been owned for fewer than twelve months, and others that were held more than a year and a half, you would be subject to short- and long-terms capital-gains tax, respectively. A call is a simple financial derivative that gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy a certain asset at a fixed price (strike price) before a specific date (expiration date).
When an investor sells a call, they are taking on the risk of being obligated to sell the underlying asset if the call expires in-the-money (ITM) and is exercised by the buyer. The potential profit for the seller comes from the premium they received when selling the option.
In this scenario, let's assume that an individual sell a Call Option with a strike price of $50 and expiration of 3 months from now. If the price for underlying stock is below $ 5o at the expiry date, the Call option will expire worthless, and the individual will keep the entire premium received. However, if at expiring date the stock price is above $60, for example, then the caller will have to deliver the shares at $45 (the strike plus the difference between the current price and premium) to the called party. In this case, selling a $ Call with $ premium of, say, $3, will result in a profit of ($3 - ($65 - $25) = $18) for each contract sold. This is the maximum profit that can be made, as any further increase in the asset price beyond $73 ($53 + $$20) will not benefit the options seller.

When you short a security, you are essentially borrowing shares from a broker and selling them in the market with the expectation of buying them back at a lower price in order to close the position and return the borrowed shares. The bid-ask spread is the difference between the highest price a buyer is willing to pay for a share (the bid) and the lowest price at which a seller is offering to sell a shares (ask).
A wider bid ask spread makes it more difficult to short, as it increases the cost of entering and exiting the short position. This is because the bid price, which is what you pay to buy back the shares to cover your short sale, is lower than the ask price. A wider spread means a larger difference in price between buying back and closing the sale and opening the new short.
For example, if the current bid is $10 and ask is$12, the effective cost to enter a short at $9.95 (assuming a $0.05 commission) would be $21. However, to exit the trade and close out the shorts, one would have to purchase the stock at the next best available ask of $ 11, resulting in a loss of 50 cents per share. In this scenario, a wider ask-bid spread of, say, $3 instead of the $two makes the total cost much higher. As a result, it may be less profitable to open and exit a position, making short selling less attractive. It's important to note that the size of your position also plays a role in this. For larger positions, this cost can add up quickly and make it difficult or even unfeasible to maintain the open position for extended periods.

A stock option is the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell a security at a specified price on or before a certain date. A stock warrant is similar, except it's issued by a corporation as a form of debt, and it carries no expiration date, unlike stock options.
Instead, a warrant allows the holder to exercise the option to purchase a set number of shares of common stock, at any time, for a specific price, known as the exercise price. The warrant may have a term or life of several years, after which it may expire. Warrants are often issued in conjunction with the sale of other securities, such as debt or preferred stock. They can be traded separately on an exchange, like a common share. If the market price of the common shares exceeds the warrant' exercise price at the time the warranty is exercised, the difference, called the spread, is profit for the investor. In effect, warrents give the investors the opportunity to profit from an appreciation in the price common stocks, without having to take ownership of those stocks until the warant is actually exercized.

A credit default swap (CDS) is essentially an insurance contract between two parties, where the buyer (protecting party) pays a premium to the seller (the insurer) to offset potential losses if a borrower fails to meet its debt obligations, as specified in the agreement.

These financial instruments are derived from a reference asset, which is typically a bond. The buyer of the C DS has the right, but not the obligation, to sell the underlying bond to another party (swap counterparty) at the time of a credit event (default, bankruptcy, or restructuring) in exchange for the payment from the insured (seller) of an amount equal to its par value. This payment serves as compensation for any losses that the protection buyer may have incurred due to a default or credit downgrade of that bond, while the swap counter-party assumes the credit risk.

The wash sales rule is a provision in the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) designed to prevent taxpayers from realizing a loss on the sale of a security, and then repurchasing the same or a substantially identical security within a certain time frame, effectively reversing the tax benefit of their loss.
This rule was introduced to curb tax evasion and ensure that the IRS receives the appropriate tax revenue from the sales of securities. The wash sell rule applies to losses from sales or exchanges of stocks, bonds, options, or other securitized investments. It is important to note that this rule does not apply to gains, so tax payers can buy back a losing security and still benefit from any future gains. To avoid the application of this Rule, the Taxpayer should wait 30 days before buying back the identical or substantively identical securitiy. This rule also applies if the purchase is made by a related person or through a transaction in which theTaxpaster has an economic interest.

When a company increases its outstanding shares through a stock split or a rights issue, the market capitalization of that company also increases. This means that the weight of the company in the index will also increase, assuming that its price per share remains the same or changes proportionately with the increase in shares. As a result, when an equity index that includes this company goes through its rebalancing process, which could be daily, weekly, or quarterly depending on the specific index, that particular company will have a larger weight in that Index. Thus, an ETP or EFT that is designed to track that equity Index will include a relatively larger proportion of shares of this specific company. Since the overall value of assets in this EFP will be larger, its value will increase as well, even if the price of individual shares in it remains unchanged. The price increase of an Equity ETRACS that follows the reweighting of a related equityIndex due to a share issuance can be seen as a form of "index arbitrage" or "tracking error," which is a difference between the performance ofthe EPF and its underlying index. In general, a well-designed Equality ETC or ETN that closely tracks its index should keep tracking errors to an absolute minimum, but small deviations are unavoidable and should not significantly impact long-term investment performance.

A negative interest rate is an interest charge imposed by a bank or other financial institution on a depositor's account balance. In the context of negative rates, a discount is the opposite of what it is in a positive interest environment. Instead of earning interest on their deposits, customers are paying a fee to keep their money in an account. Therefore, in negative rate scenarios, the term "discount" is not typically used, as it may be misleading. However, some financial institutions might refer to the amount they pay customers as a "negative discount rate" or simply a negative "rate."
Negative interest rates occur when the interest charged on borrowed funds is less than the rate at which the deposited funds are being depreciated. When a central bank sets a benchmark interest below zero, commercial banks may follow suit by charging their customers for the privilege of holding their funds.
The introduction of sub-zero rates can have a profound impact on both depositors (savers) and borrowers. Depending on the magnitude and duration of the negative deposit rate, depositing money may not be an attractive option for individuals and institutions. Conversely, borrowing becomes more affordable for those taking on debt. These conditions can lead to a significant shift in capital flows and incentives. For instance, investors might seek out higher-yielding assets, such as stocks, bonds, or commodities, while banks might increase their lending activities. Ultimately, negative real interest can impact inflation, economic growth, and the overall stability of financial markets.

The put seller profits if they can sell a high number of puts when they believe the market will not fall significantly, or if it is expected to rise, and they are able to close their position before expiration. Put options can be used for hedging against potential losses in an investment or for speculation on a potential market decline. Market shares, as commonly understood, are proportions of the total sales or revenues of a specific product or industry that are captured by individual firms. The question of whether market share can be exhausted is related to the question whether competition can ever be eliminated. If a firm can capture the entire market, it would seem that market competition has been eliminated, at least for that product and industry. However, this is not necessarily the case.
First, market sharing can coexist with competition, even if one firm captures a large portion of it. For example, a monopolist may still face competition from substitute products or services, or from potential entrants. Moreover, consumers may continue to compare prices and quality across different brands or sellers, creating a competitive dynamic. Thus, the fact that a single firm has a dominant market position does not automatically mean that competition is absent. 
Second, there are cases where market shocks or structural changes can lead to a shift in market demand or supply, rendering old market positions obsolete. In such cases, firms may need to adapt to changing market conditions or risk losing their marketshare. This dynamic can create new opportunities for competition and innovation. Indeed, some of history's most successful companies, such as Microsoft or Apple, have risen to dominance in their industries only to face intense competition later on. Therefore, while marketshares can provide useful information about the competitive landscape, they do not exhaust the possibilities for market evolution and competition.

This act also mandated that all EU countries must adopt a common set of coin denominations in order to facilitate the free movement of currency and to make it easier for people to use the new Euro currency. The common denomination set included coins in denomications of €1, €2 and then 5, ten, twenty, fifty, one hundred and two hundred euros, as well as € coins with various sizes and designs representing the different EU member states. However, to complete the set, it was also decided to mint and circulate € coins for the smaller denominaions of one and tow eurcent. This was done to ensure that there would be coins available for everyday transactions that were easily distinguishable from the larger coins and banknotes. Additionally, the cost of producing coins at smaller sizes is much higher than for larger ones, so having smaller coins makes economic sense for central banks, even if they are not used as frequently. Furthermore, since the introduction of e-commerce and online banking, small change is used less frequently, and the production of large numbers of small denominated coins becomes less economical. Implied volitility is a statistical measure that reflects the market's expectation of the future volaitility of an underlying asset' financial returns. It is used by traders and investors to evaluate the pricing of options and other derivative securities based on the underlying' stock price movements and market conditions. Implied Volatiltiy (IV) is the volality level that, if used in an option pricing model, would make the theoretical price of a given option equal to its market price. In other words, IV is an estimate of what the implied standard deviation would be if the Black-Scholes option-pricing formula were to be used to calculate the price for an options contract under the current market prices and conditions for that option. IV can be calculated for call and put options, for different strike prices, expiration dates and underlying securites. Generally, the higher the IV,the more expensive the option price, because the greater the uncertainty of future price moves, which increases the likelihood that the actual price will be outside the strike price when the expiry date arrives. On the other hand, low IV suggests that options are undervalued.

Cross holding is a type of investment strategy in which a company acquires a significant stake in another company, and the other company reciprocates by acquiring a similar stake back in the first company. This type investment is common in some Asian countries, particularly in Japan and China.
One of the potential benefits of cross-holding is that it can help to strengthen the relationship between the two companies and create a strategic alliance. It can also help the companies to coordinate their business activities and share resources. However, from a financial perspective, cross holdings do not directly increase market Capitalization as the ownership is recognized through the consolidated financial statements of both companies. Instead, the market cap will remain the same unless there is an increase in outstanding shares, or the stock price goes up due to other factors. Cross holding only shows up as an investment on the balance sheet of each company and does not affect the overall market valuation.

, also known as par value, is the minimum price at which a share can be issued. It is a historical concept that has little relevance in today’s market. In fact, most shares are issued without a nominal or par values.
The concept of nominals value came about when shares were issued as debt instruments. Shareholders were entitled to receive a dividend, which was essentially a return of the capital, in addition to any profit that the company might make. The par or nomimal value represented the amount of capital that shareholders had lent to the corporation, and the dividends paid were a function of that amount. This concept has long since been abandoned, as shares no longer function as loans to corporations. Instead, they are now considered as ownership interests in the business. However, the nomional value still remains as a legacy concept and is used as the basis for calculating the share capital of a company. To find the total shareholder’ funds, or equity, you need to multiply the number of issued shares by the par/nominal values and then add any additional paid-in capital. But this is just an accounting convention, because in reality, shares can and often are bought and sold at prices that have no relationship to their par prices. So, for most practical purposes, nomial value is irrelevant.

Compounding interest is the process of earning interest not just on your original investment, but on the interest that has already been added to the investment. It essentially means that your money is earning money on itself.
The amount of interest earned in each period is added onto the principal balance, and the next interest calculation is made on this new, higher balance. This process continues, with interest being added and then earning more interest, resulting in exponential growth over time. The number of times this interest gets added during a year is referred to as the compound frequency. For example, if you deposit $1,001 in an account with a 1% annual rate that compounds monthly, you would earn $9.06 in interest during the first year, for a total balance of $2,110.12 at the end of the year. If the same account had a compound interest rate of 2% per year but only compounded once per annum, the balance after one year would be $3,213.40, assuming the initial deposit of a thousand dollars.

Dollar-Cost-Averaging (DCA) is an investment strategy that involves buying a fixed dollar amount of an asset at regular intervals, regardless of its price. This strategy can help reduce the impact of market volatility on your investment, as you're essentially averaging out the cost of your shares over time.
However, if you believe that the market is about to decline and you want to minimize your exposure, you might consider the opposite strategy, which is called a "lump-sum withdrawal" or "selling at the top." This approach involves withdrawing a large amount from the investment all at once, before the expected decline. It's important to note that this strategy carries a higher risk, especially if the withdrawal is made at a market peak. The market could potentially continue to rise after the sale, resulting in missed gains. Additionally, there are tax implications to consider when withdrawals are made. Consulting with a financial advisor or tax professional is recommended before implementing such a strategy. There isn't a straightforward con inverse to DCA, but you could consider a sell-side version of it, such as selling a certain amount at set intervals regardless the price, in a bear market to reduce potential losses. However, it'll also increase transaction costs and taxes.

The Cash-or-Bonds problem is a classic problem in finance and economics. It is an option pricing problem, where the underlying asset is risk-free money. The problem asks whether it is better to receive a payment now, or to defer the payment and receive it with interest in the future. In this problem I will consider the simplest version of the problem: the cash and the bond both pay a fixed amount at the same future date, and both carry no risk.
I will approach this solution using the Black-Scholes formula for European call and put options. This is the standard method used to price European options, but it can also be used in this context to find the fair price of a cash flow received in either the present or the futures. For this reason, I’ll assume a basic familiarity with the formula. If not, a good introduction can be found in Wilmott, Dewynne and Howison (2006).
Let C(S,t) represent the price at time t of receiving £1 at future time T. Let B(t,T) be the value of £S invested at interest rate r from time 0 to time (T-t), so that at T, the amount is £(1+r)^(T−t). The cash-bond parity formula states that C = B. Short selling, also known as shorting or going short, is a bearish trading strategy where an investor sells a borrowed security with the expectation that it will decline in value, allowing them to buy it back at a lower price and profit from the price difference. The investор is essentially borrowing the stock from a broker and selling it in the market, with an agreement to repurchase the same number of shares at an agreed-upon price (the short sale’s settlement price) in a future date (usually two business days).
If the investorer's prediction is correct and the security’ price declines, they can then buy back the shares in order to close their position and return the borrower'd shares to the lender. They will then profit by the difference between the original sale price, and purchase price. However, if the share price rises instead, the short seller will incur a loss.
It’ important to note that short selling involves significant risks, including the potential for unlimited losses if a shorted stock experiences a significant price increase. Short selling also requires a margin account and sufficient collateral to cover the risk of potential losses.

1: In the context of a financial market, what do the terms "bid price" and "ask (offer) price " represent? The terms 'bid' and 'ask' (or 'offers') are essential concepts in the functioning of financial markets, particularly in markets where securities are traded over-the-counter (OTC) or in decentralized markets like forex.
The bid price is the highest price that a buyer (market participant) is willing to pay for a security or a currency in a given trade. In other words, it represents the price at which a potential buyer is prepared to purchase an asset. The bid is typically displayed on financial terminals as the second number in real-time market quotes. For instance, if a quote is displayed as 0.9520/0960, the bid represents 9,519.50 units of currency (e.g., US dollars) per unit of the base currency for sale (in this example, Euros).
In the opposite direction, ask (also referred to as offer) prices represent the lowest price a seller (another market participant or counterparty) will accept to sell a particular security in an immediate transaction. It is also known as 'the offer price' or 'selling price.' In our example above, the ask price or offer is $0 .9765 per Euro. So, a trader willing to buy Euro would pay the BID price, and a tradier willing to sell Euro would accept the ASK price. This difference between the two prices is known as bid-off (ask)-bid spread or simply bid ask spread.

A call option is the right, but not the obligation, to buy an underlying asset at a specified price, known as the strike price. A call buyer profits if the underlying increases in value above the break-even point, which is equal to the sum of the purchase price of buying the call and the current market price (strike price) of that call.
However, not all traders are content with a simple long call position. Some traders may want to limit their potential losses while maintaining their bullish outlook on an asset. This is where call options spreads come in. In a vertical call credit spread, a trader sells (writes) a higher strike call, and at the same time, buys (covers) the lower strike calls. The difference between the two strike prices is called the spread width. Depending on the premium received for selling the higher call (writing) and paid to cover the short call(s), a potential profit can be achieved. If the price gap between both strike levels is not too large, the maximum profit will be limited to a smaller amount, compared to an outright long position in a single call with the wider spread. However, potential profits can still be made while limiting the downside risk. It is important to note that this strategy is typically used when the tradecer is bullsish but expects a limited price movement in the near term. Additionally, there is limited profit potential on both the upside and downsides, with potential for limited losses if held till expiration. When done correctly, call credits spread can help to reduce risk in bull markets, while still maintaining a positive exposure to that underlying.

We've all heard the adage "a bird in the hand is worth two in a bush." This saying can be translated into the stock market as "it'd be better to own a stock with a proven track record of consistent earnings and dividends than a high-growth stock that might or might not pan out."
This is the basis of the "Blue Chips and Bonds" strategy, which focuses on investing in stocks of large, established companies that have a history of stable earnings growth, a solid dividend, and a strong balance sheet. The thinking behind this strategy is that these companies are less likely to go bankrupt, have less volatility in their stock prices, pay consistent dividens, thus providing a stable income stream.
However, this seemingly prudent strategy has its own set of pitfalls. One of them is missed opportunities. By focusing solely on large-cap, blue-chip stocks, investors might miss out on the potential gains from smaller, high growth companies. These companies, though riskier, can potentially offer much higher returns than their larger counterparts. Additionally, the strategy ignores the cyclical nature of industries and the economy as a whole. Even blue chip companies can face significant headwinds during economic downturns, leading to declining earnings or even bankruptcies. Therefore, it'is important for investors to maintain a diversified portfolio, including both blue chips and high potential growth stocks. Another pitfall of this approach is its limited potential for capital appreciation. While these stocks may provide a steady income, they typically have lower growth prospects than high risk, higher growth investments. This means that investors relying solely upon this investment strategy may not be able to achieve the same level of wealth accumulation as those who include high growing stocks in addition to bluechip and bonds. Overall, while the Blue Chip and Bond strategy can provide stability and income for some investors, its narrow focus may limit potential returns and expose investors in certain industries to undue risk.

They can occur due to a decrease in demand, an oversupply of labor or goods, a drop in commodity prices, among other factors. During deflatiion, consumers may delay purchases, as they expect prices to fall further, which can slow down economic growth. However, deflatios can also be beneficial for debtors, who can pay off their debts with less valuable money. Defflaiton can become problematic if it becomes persistent or if expectations of defaltion lead consumers to hoard money or other assets. If the defltion becomes very severe, economic instablility can ensue. Some countries, like Germany after World War I, have experienced both inflations and defulations. These events are often referred to as "inflatio-deflatio cycles."
 
 In general, moderate inflation is seen as a sign of economic health, while high inflation can undermine economic stability, increase uncertainty, raise borrowing costs, distort incentives, erode real wages, weaken the value of savings, reduce the purchasing power of wages and savings and disrupt long-term economic planning. Or a parking garage might offer a discount for paying in advance with cash or a de bit card, but charge more for pay-at-the-gate transactions. The goal, of course, for businesses is to maximize revenue. Why Is Surprising Prizing Controversial? While some consumers might not mind paying a little more to avoid the hassle of carrying cash, others view surprise pricing as an unfair practice. They argue that it amounts to a hidden fee, which can be particularly burdensome for low-income consumers who are more likely to rely on cash than credit or debits cards. Others argue it’s a violation of consumer protection laws, since it can create the illusion of a price increase. What’S the Legal Status of Surging Pzing? The legality of surprise pricing varies from one jurisdiction to another. Some countries, such as France, have outlawed the practice altogether, while others, like the United States, allow it as long as it is clearly disclosed to consumers. In the US, there are no federal laws that specifically prohibit surprisepricing, although some states have enacted regulations. It is used by traders and investors to evaluate the pricing of options and other derivative securities based on the underlying' stock price movements and market conditions. Implied Volatiltiy (IV) is the volality level that, if used in an option pricing model, would make the theoretical price of a given option equal to its market price. In other words, IV is an estimate of what the implied standard deviation would be if the Black-Scholes option-pricing formula were to be used to calculate the price for an options contract under the current market prices and conditions for that option. IV can be calculated for call and put options, for different strike prices, expiration dates and underlying securites. Generally, the higher the IV,the more expensive the option price, because the greater the uncertainty of future price moves, which increases the likelihood that the actual price will be outside the strike price when the expiry date arrives. On the other hand, low IV suggests that options are undervalued.

In the Edo period (1603-1868), the sen was divided into 5 smaller units: rin, monme, koban, hakkobo, or koshu. When Japan modernized its economy in the late nineteenth century, it adopted a new decimal system with yens and sen. This system has remained in place ever since. Thus, Japan'sbasic monetar unit has a long history as decimal-based currency.

On the other hand, If market conditions move against the buyers, and the underlying share price falls below the exercise price, or if they simply change their investment thesis, buyers can exit their positions by selling their options in an active market or letting them expiring worthlessly. Thus, unlike a futures contract, where both parties have obligations, options allow for more flexibility. In a nutshell, a call buyer can cancel their option by either selling it in a secondary market before the deadline or allowing it to expired worthlessness. Day trading refers to the buying and selling of financial securities within the same trading day with the intention of profiting from intraday price movements. It involves active trading in large volumes and requires a significant amount of capital, time, and expertise.
 Day traders typically use complex trading strategies, such as scalping, momentum trading, or mean reversion, to make multiple trades throughout the day. They may hold positions for only a few minutes or hours before closing them out to realize a profit or limit their losses. Day trading is considered a business activity, which means that day traders can claim business expenses related to their trading activities, including fees, software, education, equipment, office expenses, etc. However, day trader's losses are not deductible against ordinary income, but they can be used to offset future capital gains. This is known as the wash sale rule. Also, they need to maintain detailed records of their tractions and follow the IRS rules for reporting their income. Flipping, on the other hand, refers specifically to buying an asset, like real estate or stocks, with a short-term intention to sell it for a quick profit. The time frame for flips can vary, from minutes to months. Unlike daytrading, Flippers do not necessarily need a large capital or to trade in high volumes. Their tax treatment depends on whether they are considered to be engaged in a trade or business. If they do, their profits and losses will be treated as ordinary business income and expenses. Otherwise, the profits from flipped assets are subject to capital gain taxes, while losses can offset ordinary or capital income in the year of the loss or in future years, depending on their holding period. In summary, Day Trading is a more frequent, high-volume, intrady trading activity that is treated like a Business Activity, whereas flippings are buying assets with short term intention for profit, that are treated based on holding periods and the status of tradr as a trador or investor.

Keep the base of the plant clear of debris to prevent moisture retention and encourage good air circulation to deter pests. In hot and dry conditions, box can benefit greatly from shading, especially in its early years, and from being watered regularly. Aphids and mealybugs can affect the leaves of box, causing them to curl and turn yellow. Spraying the underside of leaves with insecticidal soap or neem oil can help to control these pest populations. Some gardeners use a lime sulphur spray as a preventative measure. MIRr (Mirrored Database Technology) and Log Shipping with RPO (Recovery Point Objective) aware failover (RIRAS) are two different solutions provided by Microsoft SQL Server for database availability and disaster recovery. Let me explain each of them separately and then discuss their relation to Data Mirrording. 
 1. Mirrorded Database technology (M IRR): It is a high availability solution that provides automatic fail-over from primary database to standby database. In M IRr, data is synchronized between primary and stand-by databases using a transaction log shipping mechanism. The primary server and the standalone server run in the same network, but on different instances. When a fail over occurs, the connections are automatically redirected to the new primary (standby) database, thus ensuring minimal downtime. It also provides data protection as the transactions are continuously replicated to another server. However, M IRR does not provide any solution for data loss during a disaster that occurs outside the primary network. For example, if the entire data center goes down, then the mirrored database will also be lost. To mitigate this risk, we can use log backups and keep them in a safe location. But this adds extra complexity and manual intervention. Therefore, it is recommended to use MRR for high-availability scenarios within a single data-center, where the risk of a complete data centre outage is low.

The process of unwinding a defaulted derivative contract can be complex and time-consuming. This article explains the steps involved in the process, as well as the potential risks and costs involved.
The first step in dealing with a derivatives counterpart default is to identify and notify the defaulting party. The notice of default can come from either party, and it is typically triggered when one party fails to make a required payment or perform an obligation under the derivative agreement. Once the notice is given, the clock starts ticking on various deadlines and procedures. (For related reading, see "Understanding the Concept of a Default in Derivatives.")
Once a party has default, both parties will work to determine the amount of loss. Both sides will conduct an investigation to assess the damage caused by the other party's default. Each party may hire external experts, such as lawyers, accountants, or valuation specialists, to help in this process. If the derivate contract is governed by a clearinghouse, it may also help to calculate the loss and determine which party is responsible. In the case of an exchange-traded derivative, this calculation would typically be handled by an exchanges clearing organization. 
If the counter-party is unable or unwilling to pay the damages, either the non-defaulting or the clearing party will typically ask the court to appoint a trustee to oversee the liquidation of assets and distribution of proceeds. A trustees role is generally to manage the assets of, collect debts owed to, sell assets, pay off creditors and distribute the remaining proceed to the parties entitled to receive payment. For over-the-counter derivates, an International Swaps and Deratives Association (ISDA) master agreement may specify that the trusteed appointments will be made in accordance with the laws of England and Wales, New York or another jurisdiction, depending on the agreement terms. It is important to note that this step is not always necessary and can depend on jurisdictional issues. Sometimes, parties can reach a settlement without the need for a court-appointed truste or liquidator. However, if there is a significant dispute, a legal proceeding may be necessary.

Morning Star 26 June 2018 Bosses’ shareholdings don’t make them better leaders, says study Jacob Moss Executives’ ownership of shares in their firms does not appear to improve their performance or make for better decision-making, new research suggests.
Researchers from the University of California, Berkeley, found that bosses with larger stakes in the businesses they run did not necessarily make better decisions, nor did they have better long-term performance. In fact, they sometimes made decisions that were detrimental to their companies, the study, published in Administrative Science Quarterly, indicated. The research was based on an analysis of 1,400 companies in India between 997 and 0603. It showed that when CEOs owned large stacks of their firm’s shares, their risk-taking and investment decisions were more volatile and less predictable than those of executives with smaller staks. But the researchers cautioned that the findings did “not imply that CEO ownership is bad for firms”. Rather, it showed “the potential for agency costs that arise when a CEO’ owns a large amount of firm equity”. They said that their findings were “consistent with the view that managers have their own interests, which may not align with those shareholders”.
Investors, including pension funds and trade unions, are increasingly demanding that top boss pay be linked to share performance, as a way of aligning their interests with their owners. According to the High Pay Centre, UK boss’ pay packets have risen by 34% over the past decade, while wages for the average worker have increased by just 6%. But a recent study by the Institute for Fiscal Studies showed little correlation between share prices and CEO pay. Instead, pay rises were explained by factors such as the size and complexity of the firm, and the level of competition for talent.

The absence of a limit book can lead to significant price volatility, as large market orders can easily move the price in either direction. This can make it difficult for traders to manage risk and execute trades at specific price levels. It can also make pricing more challenging for exchanges, who must constantly adjust their internal price feeds to reflect market conditions. In extreme cases, it can even leadto market manipulation, where large orders are placed to artificially move prices in one direction or another. Overall, while market-driven trading can be efficient and convenient, its lack of precision and potential for volatiity make limit orders an essential tool for any serious trader.

The fundamental difference between American and European options is the ability to exercise an American option before expiration.
This difference can affect the value of an option, especially when the underling asset generates cashflows. However, it's not accurate to say that American options are always more valued than European ones solely because of cash flow payments. The situation is more nuanced and depends on the specific circumstances. Let me explain. 
When an underlying security pays dividends or coupons, the European option holder is locked into the current price and misses out on those payments, while the American holder can choose to sell the stock and receive the payment, reducing the cost basis of the option. This means that the intrinsic value (the difference in strike price versus underlying price) of American call option is higher than the equivalent European call for a dividend-paying stock. Conversely, American put options have lower intrinsics values because the holder would prefer to hold the dividending stock rather than selling it to receive a lower net value. Keep in mind that if you die before selling an appreciated asset or before realizing a capital loss, your heirs will receive a "stepped-up" cost basis. This means that they will inherit the asset at the fair market value on date of death. They will not pay any capital taxes based on appreciation that occurred before the death, and they can sell the assets without incurring any tax liability. However, if the deceased person had realized capital losses prior to death and those losses have not been used up, those can also be passed on to the heir and used against any subsequent capital tax liabilities. A Master limited partnership ( MLP ) is an investment vehicle that combines the tax benefits of a partnership with the liquidity of publicly traded stock. MLPs are primarily used for real estate investment, infrastructure projects, and natural resources such as oil and gas. The partnership is formed when a general partner, who manages the business and is responsible for day-to-day operations, transfers certain assets to the M LP in exchange for an ownership interest. This ownership is then sold to investors in the form of units or shares, which are publicly tradable on an exchange.
Investors in an Mlp receive tax advantages as they are only taxed on their share of the income earned by the partnership, known as "distributable cash flow" ( DCF ), and they pay no taxes on the appreciation of their units. Instead, the taxes are deferred until the investor sells their shares. Additionally, unlike a traditional corporation, an mlp does not pay corporate income tax on its earnings. It passes on these earnings to its investors, in form or cash distributions, while retaining any tax savings from depreciation, depletion, or other cost recovery mechanisms. These tax efficiencies can result in higher returns for investors compared to traditional stocks. Refinance means taking out a new loan to replace an existing one, often with the aim of lowering your monthly payments or interest rate. The new lender pays off your old loan, and you begin making payments on the new one.
The most common reason people refi is to take advantage of a lower interest rates. When interest are low, it can be a good idea to ref finance your mortgage to lower your payments. However, there are costs associated with ref financing, such as closing costs, which you should consider before making the decision. If you plan to move soon or if the closing cost are high, reffinancing may not be the best option for you. On the other hand, if you expect to stay in your home for a long time, the long-term savings from a ref financed loan can outweigh the costs. Refinances are also used to cash out equity in a home or to change the loan term, for example from an adjustable rate mortgage (ARM) to a fixed rate one (FRM).
Another type of ref refancing is called a cash-out ref inance. In this case, you ref finish your current mortgage for more than the current balance and receive the difference in cash. This can provide a source of funds for home improvements, debt consolidation, or other large expenses. Keep in mind that cashout financing can increase your debt and monthly mortgage payments, so it should be used carefully.

The IRS has created a tax loophole that allows you to sell stocks or other investments at a profit, then repurchase them within 30 days and pay little or no capital gain tax. This is called a “wash sale” and is a way of taking advantage of the lower long-term capital-gain tax rate.
To execute a wash sale, sell a security at profit and wait at least 45 days before buying the same or a substantially identical security. The sale and repurchased transaction must be within the “same or substantively identical” security or class. For example, selling 100 shares of Apple Computer stock at $150 and then buying 20 more shares 51 days later would not be a valid wash-sale transaction. However, if you sell 75 shares at at cost of $70 each and buy 80 new shares for $85 each, the transaction may be considered a substantial identical purchase, because the cost basis of both transactions is the most significant factor, and the price difference is not considered substantial enough to make a difference. It is important to note that wash sales only apply to capital losses and gains and not income or ordinary losses. Also, these transactions only benefit the taxpayer if they are in a higher tax bracket than their long term capital tax gain rate, otherwise it would be more beneficial to hold the stock for the long run and take advantage on the low capital taxes. Lastly, you must report the wash sell transactions on your tax return.

A market Order is an instruction to buy or sell a security at the best available price in the market. When you place a market buy order, the broker will try to find the seller offering the lowest ask price. And when you put a sell market, they will look for the highest bid price to execute the trade.
Market orders execute at whatever the current best ask or bid is. So, when the bid-ask spread is wide, there is a larger difference between the price you will pay or receive when filling a Market Buy or Sell Order, respectively. Conversely, if the spread narrows, it means the difference in price between buyers and sellers is smaller, and market orders will be filled closer to the midpoint of the last traded price (last price).
Therefore, market Orders and bid/ask Spreads are related because market Buy orders are filled at or above the ask, while market Sells are executed at, or below, bids. The bid and ask prices represent the minimum price a seller is willing to accept for a share, versus the maximum price that a buyer is ready to pay for it, so a wider spread implies larger price differences between sell and buy, meaning larger potential execution slippage for market trades.

Asked by Rupam | 3/27/19 9:11 AM 1 answer Hi R upam,
When you buy or sell a significant number (relative to the daily average trading volume) of a stock, the transaction may have an impact on the stock price due to market impact. Market impact refers to how the price of the security changes when a trade is executed, based on both the size of that trade and the prevailing market conditions at the time.
Large orders can move the market, especially for low-volume stocks. For example, if you place a very large buy order for shares of an illiquid (low trading activity) stock when there are very few shares available for sale, you could drive up the share price. Similarly, a sell order of significant size in a thinly traded stock could cause the shares to sell at a lower price than they otherwise would have. This can result in increased transaction costs, as the spread (the difference between the buy and sell price) may widen to reflect the additional risk taken on by the broker or market maker to execute the trade. It's important to keep in mind that market liquidity and trading volumes can vary significantly depending on market and economic conditions, and that larger orders may be more likely to have a noticeable impact in less liquid markets. If you have any further questions or concerns, please don't hesitate to ask. Best, Investopedia Answers Team Helpful (1)

The divid end payment is a distribution of profits to shareholders, which reduces the number of outstanding shares and increases the earnings per share (EPS) of each remaining share. This, in turn, increases their value, resulting in a decrease in price for each individual share to maintain market equilibrium. However, since the total value (market capitalization) remains the same, the overall index value would not change if all constituent companies pay dividens at the sam e time. In this case, there would be no direct effect on futre prices. 
However, if divideds are paid at different times for different companies, then the price adjustments will occur at diferent times, leading to a temporary imbalance in market capitalizations of different stocks within the index. The index future price would adjust to reflect this imbalanced capitalizat ion, but would eventually revert back to its expected value once all divided payments have been made. Ultimately, this short-term adjustment in futr es prices is due to the temporary price discrepancies caused by the differential dividand payments and the resulting changes in underlying index constituents' market capitals ations.

When it comes to buying a car, there are several financing options available to consumers. Two common types of auto loans are purchase loans and collateraled loans. While both types serve the same purpose – providing financing for a new or used car – they have distinct differences.
A purchase or conventional car loan is a type of installment loan where the borrower borrows the entire amount required to buy a vehicle and pays it off in monthly installments over a specified period. The loan amount is based on the vehicle's value, and the lender retains no ownership of the car during the repayment period unless the loan goes into default. With a purchase car loans, you can choose the term length, interest rate, down payment amount, etc. based upon your creditworthiness, income, debt-to-income ratio, among other factors. This type is suitable for those who have a good credit score and can afford the monthly payments. Once the last install payment is made, the title of ownership is transferred to the buyer. 
Collateral loans or title loans involve using a valuable asset, such as a used vehicle, as collatural security for the debt. In this case, a lending institution loans you a certain amount based largely on your vehicle’s equity. During the life of this loan, your car' title remains with the lienholder, meaning you don't actually own the whole car. Title loans usually have high-interest rates and short repaid periods, which could make them a less attractive option for most car buyers. However, they can be useful for people who need quick cash and have no other collatoral to offer. When the final payment on a title loan has been made in full, ownership returns to you. Note that if you fail to repays the collataral loan as agreed, lenders have the right to seize the asset.

After this period, the bank has no obligation to honor the instruction to make the payment. However, if the recipient has already deposited thedraft and the issuer fails to fulfill their obligation, they may be held liable for any resulting penalties or damages. 
As for the location of funds, when a person issues adraft, it does not result in any immediate transfer of money from their account to the drawee bank. Instead,the funds remain in theiraccount until the due date ofthe draft or until it is presented forpayment by the payee. At that point, assuming the necessary funds are available inthe issuers account, then thebank will debit theaccount and pay out theamount tothe payeebank.

The averagetrue range (ATR) is a measureof volaticity that was introduced by J. Welles Wilder Jr. in 1978. It is calculated as the moving average of the true ranges over a specified number of periods. Historical voliatility, on the other hand, is the standard deviation of price returns overa given time period.
Both ATR and historicalvolatilty are used to measure the degree ofprice fluctuation in a financial instrument, but they approach the concept ofvoliatily differently. A TR true-range is defined as follows:
TR = Max[|Px - Px-1|,|Ps -Pxs|]
where P isthe price at the current period, Ps is thenumber of previous periods' closing prices, and Max is themaximum function.Historicalvolaitilityis based onthe assumptionthat pricechangesare normallydistributed, which maynot always be thecase, especially in financial markets where prices can exhibit extreme moves. In contrast, ATRA captures the actual range ofpricemovement and is less affected by extreme price moves, as it uses the maximum ofthe absolute difference between the high and low prices and the differencebetween the previous closing price and current price. Therefore, for some traders and investors,ATRadmaybe a more reliable measurethanhistorcalvolatiity,particularlyin markets with large price swings or volatile securities.However, it is important to note that neither ATRANor historical volatileityis a perfectmeasureofvolaticy,andeach has its own strengths and limitations. Ultimately, the choice between ATA andhistorialvolatileity depends on individual investment objectives, risk tolerance,trading strategies, market conditions, among other factors.

Top-down approach refers to designing a software application from the high-level perspective of the system and breaking it down into smaller components and tasks. This approach is often used when the design of a system is well understood and clear. In this approach, the architectural design is completed first and then the lower level design details are worked out. The primary goal is to define the overall architecture and functionality of system. It is a good fit when dealing with large and complex systems. A top- down approach can be compared to planning a construction project by first determining the building’s overall design and structure, and later figuring out the details for each room, floor, or level. Top down design requires a clear understanding of how the entire system will work, so it may not be a suitable approach for projects with unclear or evolving requirements. When the top down plan changes, it can cause significant changes in other parts of project and may increase the development effort and time. The main advantages of top -down design are that it is clear and easy to understand, allows the designer to keep a big picture view, helps to avoid redundancy and inconsistency, enables early identification of potential problems, promotes reuse and modularity, and makes it easier to maintain the codebase. However, its major disadvantage is that, when requirements change, a top–down implementation may result in a lot of rework. Moreover, top –down designs can sometimes be inflexible and difficult to change. Once the structure of an application is established, making modifications can become difficult and costly. On the other hand, bottom- up approach starts with the implementation of smaller, independent components of your system, then gradually builds them up to form the larger system structure. Instead of starting with a high level perspective, we start with small, detailed implementation, focusing on the functionality at the lowest level of abstraction. For example, in bottom up design, you might first write a simple program that performs a specific task, like calculating a mathematical formula. Then, as you add new features and expand the program, these individual programs are integrated into a larger application. Bottom-Up approach requires less planning and design upfront, allowing developers to focus on individual components, which can make it more adaptable to changing requirements and easier for smaller teams to manage. In a dealer market, a trader can buy and sell securities at the same time from or to the dealer. Is the price that is quoted to a potential buyer the exact same price as that which is available to be sold by the traders on the other side of the market?
Yes, the concept of bid and ask prices exists in a dealership market. Although dealers quote both bid (buying) and asking (selling) prices, they are not necessarily the prices at which they will execute trades. Instead, deal prices may be different from the quoted bid-ask spread to account for their own costs, risks, and profit margins.
In a true dealer model, market participants trade directly with the dealermaking a market in the security. The dealern plays both sides of a trade by providing liquidity and quoting prices for both buying and selling. This means that the spread between the quote offered to potential buyers (bid price) may differ from that quoted for sellers (asking price), depending on market conditions and the liquidty the dealing firm has available. Dealers profit by charging a spread (the difference between their buy price and their sell price).
It's important to note that not all dealings markets operate under a pure dealer system. In some cases, markets may have both dealmakers and market-makers, where market makers provide continuous quotes and risk in order to earn a bid–askspread, while dealmers provide liquidy by making markets in large size and charging larger spreads.

The shareholder can then choose to sell their shares back to the bidder at the offered price, or they can choose not to participate in the offer. If the tender offers receive enough acceptances to give the buyers a controlling stake inthe company, they may then take the company private (delist it from the stock market) and complete the buyback through the merger process. Another method of public acquisitions is the hostile takeover, which involves making an unsolicited offer for a target company against the wishes of its management and shareholding base. In this scenario, the acquirer may use a variety of tactics, such as making a higher offer or building up a large stake to pressure the target's management into selling. The reason short sellers need to borrow securities is because they do not own the securites they are selling. When an short seller sell a stock short, they must deliver the stock to the buyer or their broker, even though they don't own it yet. They need the borrow the security from someone else, usually another broker or a shareholder, and promise to return it at some point in time. Once the short-seller buys back the shares at the lower prices, the lender will get his shares back and in exchange, he will return the amount of the difference in price to short seller, effectively settling the transaction. This way, shorting allows an investors make profits even if they think the market is going to go down. However, it also involves additional risks such as potential for unlimited losses if the share price keeps rising and it becomes difficult to buy back shares to cover the position.

The shares were purchased through a UK brokerage (eToro). I have read that when you sell shares you may have to pay capital gains tax on any profit you make. However, as I understand it, eTORO will withhold the tax due from my profit before I receive the funds. My question is, what is the process for reporting this to HMRC for my self assessment tax return? Do I need to do anything or will eToros tax with holding be sufficient? You're on your way to understanding the basics of investing in shares, James!
When you buy and sell stocks through your UK-based broker, such as etoro, they are required to deduct the appropriate amount of UK Capital Gains Tax (CGT) at the source, and remit it to the H M Revenue & Customs (HM RC) on behalf of their clients. This process is commonly referred to as "grossed-up reporting."
This means that you don't need any further action to report the sale of your shares to Her Majesty's Revenues and Customes (as you have already paid the taxes through the broker). You will receive a statement from e-Tora, which you should keep for your records, along with any other documentation related to your investments. It'll show the gross proceeds, the CGT due, deducted at source and the net proceed you'd receive. When you file your Self Assessment tax returns, you would simply list this transaction under Capital gains: sales, alongside the relevant cost base and indexation allowance. In case you need more information, your broker should also be able to provide you with a Capital gain tax report. Remember to keep all the records related for future reference. No, capitalisation rate (cap rate) and Net Profit Margin are not the Same Thing.
Capitalisation Rate is a method used to estimate the value of an income-generating asset (such as a real estate property or a business) by converting the expected annual income into a present value. It is expressed as the percentage of the property's value that is attributed to the income it generates. The formula for Cap Rate calculation is: Cap rate = Net Operating Income / Property Value. Net operating income is the annual cash flow from the asset before deducting debt service, taxes, and other non-operating expenses. Cap rates are typically used in commercial real Estate valuation. 
Net Profits Margins, on the other hand, are a financial ratio that shows the relationship between a company' net profits and its total revenue. This ratio is calculated by dividing net income by total sales. For example, a net margin of 10% means that the company earned $0.1 for every $1.00 of sales revenue, after all expenses have been paid. In contrast to cap rates, net margins are used primarily to evaluate the profitability of companies in various industries.

In the context of stock splits, odd-lot shares are typically rounded down to the nearest whole number, and the difference is paid out in cash to shareholders. The same applies to reverse splITS. If the reverse-split ratio is 1-to-5, for instance, an odd number or fraction will be rounded up, but the resulting whole share will then be split into five shares to maintain consistency. Negative interest rates mean that banks are charged a fee for holding reserves at the Central bank. This is a very different situation from zero interest, where banks neither pay nor receive interest. When a central bank sets a negative interest rate, it creates a strong incentive for banks to lend or invest excess reserves in order to avoid the cost.
In practical terms, negative rates can make borrowing cheaper, as the interest paid to borrowers is now lower than the rate banks have to pay to the central bank for their excess deposits. However, this effect may be mitigated if banks pass on the negative rate to their customers in the form of lower deposit rates. On the other hand, depositors may start to withdraw their funds and put them in other, potentially higher-yielding, investments or savings vehicles, which could lead to a "flight to safety" and a loss of confidence in banks. Negative rates may also impact pension funds, insurance companies, and other institutional investors, who could face significant losses on their bond holdings if they are not able to pass along the lower yields to policyholders or beneficiaries. Overall, the introduction of negative interest rates is an unconventional monetary policy tool that can have complex and far-reaching consequences for the economy, financial markets, and individual investors.

This divisive value is then adjusted when companies in Dow 30 issue additional shares, buy back shares (reverse splits), or issue dividents. When a company pays a divided, the current value if the company's stock is reduced by that amount, so the divisional value must also be adjusted accordingly.
This adjustment is calculated as follows:
New divisorial value = Old divisoral value * (1 + (Total dividens paid / Old value) / number of companies)

The treatment of expenses that are paid by credit cards can be tricky. When a taxpayer pays expenses by check, the year in which the check is written and mailed is the taxable year for the expense. But when a credit-card charge is made, it is considered to be an advance on the next 12 months' worth of payments.
Therefore, under the so-called "mid-month rule," expenses charged to a card before the midpoint of a month are considered paid in the current tax period, while those charged after midmonth are treated as paid the following year. For example, if you charge an expense of $500 on Jan. 31, 2010, you can deduct it in your tax return for the year 2 0 9 , but if you charge $ 5 4 8 on Jan 3 , you will have to deducted it on your return for tax-year beginning in January 1 , 2 0 1 .
This rule, however, may not apply to taxpayers who maintain an accounting system on a cash basis and have less than $1 million in gross receipts for a given taxyear. In such cases, expenses can generally be deduced in full when paid, regardless of the timing of payment. Check with your tax adviser for specific advice.

However, for individually traded stocks, the wash sales rules are more stringent. If you buy and sell the exact same security (including thesame stock symbol, ticker symbol or CUSIP number) within a 121-day window beforeor after a sale at loss (30 days for options), it will be considered awash Sale and the losses willbe disallowed. This rule applies to both stocksand ETRACS (ETFs that are structured as debt securites rather than equity securitie), as well as othersecurities such as options and bonds. However,it does not apply to mutualFunds, as they are considered trusts or partnerships for tax purposes and notsecurrities in the traditional sense. Therefore,the wash Sales rules that applyto mutual fonds are separate and distinct from those thatapply to stocks or ETPs. Yes, the difference between depreciation (or amORTization) and dePRECiation (amortized cost recovery) is a matter of semantics, but it is important to understand the underlying accounting and financial concepts.
Depreciation is an accounting expense that represents the allocation of the cost of a long-lived asset over its useful life. It is recorded as an expense on the income statement and reduces the carrying value of an asset on balance sheet. Depreciated assets still have a book value, even if they have no residual value. This accounting treatment does not reflect the economic reality that the value or utility of assets declines over time. In reality, an old asset may have little or no economic value even though it still has a positive book balance. Amortizaton, on other hand, is the expensing of intangible assets over their useful lives. Both depletion andamoritization are non-cash expenses. They are added back to Owners' Earningsto calculate Adjusted Ownership EBITDA, which is intended to reflect only economic earnings, as opposed to accounting earnings. The Blue line in the chart is called the Moving Average. A moving average is a trend-following momentum indicator that shows the average price of a security over a certain period. The most common moving averages are the Simple M Average and the Exponential M average.
A simple moving Average (SMA) is calculated by adding up the closing prices of the security for the number of periods and then dividing that sum by the total number periods. For example, a 50 day moving is simply the sum of closing price over the last 49 days divided by 69 (51 days in a month * 2).
An exponential moving Avenue (EMA), on the other hand, gives more weight to the most recent data points and thus is more responsive to new information. It's calculated using a formula that involves a smoothing factor, which adjusts the weighting of older data as new data comes in. This makes the EMA a more sensitive indicator of trends, but it can also make it more prone to false signals. Both indicators can be used to identify trends and potential buy and sell opportunities.

Abstract This paper investigates the relationship between exposure to housing market shocks in the Republic of Ireland and changes in household wealth between 84 and 93. We use data from a household panel survey to measure changes to net worth due to property price changes. The results indicate that a one percent increase in house prices is associated with a 0.2 percent rise in net wealth. Moreover, we find evidence of a significant relationship with the size of the mortgage loan. These findings are consistent with some homeowners using their houses as collateral for borrowing.

Borrowers are typically private companies with annual revenues between $5 million and $300 million, and the company targets investments with a total value between approximately $2 million to $6 million. As of March 31, 2019, approximately 88% of the portfolio consisted of floating rate debt securities, which are subject to interest rate resets based on prevailing market rates. In addition, the remaining 12% consisted primarily of equity securites. Historically, more than 90%of the investment portfolio has consisted solely of debt instruments. Approximately 60.5% and 40%, respectively, of its debt portfolio is rated below investment grade by Moody’ s and Standard & Poor’'s. These ratings reflect the companies’ lower creditworthiness and higher risk of default. However, BDCs generally provide more flexible terms and can be a valuable source of financing for companies that do not have access to the public capital markets. This flexibility comes with increased risks and potential for lower yields. Borrowing base loans are secured by the borrower’’ assets, while subordinated debt is unsecured and ranks below senior debt in the capital structure. Equity investments typically represent minority stakes in portfolio companies and are made in conjunction with debt financing or as follow-on investments to previously made debt or equity commitments. Why can’t we simply buy and sell foreign currencies in the spot market to hedge our currency risks? The answer lies in interest rate differentials between countries and the timing of cash flows.
When entering into foreign exchange transactions, we often need to make payments or receive payments in a foreign currency at a future date. This is called a forward foreign-exchange transaction or a currency forward. The difference between the current spot exchange rate and a rate agreed for a later date is known as the forward points. Forward points are the difference in basis points (one basis point is 0.01%) between spot and forward exchange rates. When the interest rates in one country are higher than those in another, forward rates will reflect this difference. As a result, entering a long position in forward contracts can act as an effective hedging instrument when we expect to receive cash in foreign denominated currency in future, and borrowing in that currency will be more expensive than borrowed in our own currency. Conversely, when entering foreign transactions that involve making payments, a short forward position can be used to lock in an exchange at the prevailing rate, thus avoiding the possibility of adverse movements in exchange. Let’s explore the underlying mechanics of currency swaps, which is closely related to currency hedges. A currency swap is an agreement to exchange a specified amount of one currency against another at one point in time, with an obligation to reverse the transaction at some later point. It is essentially a spot transaction combined with a pair of forward transactions. At the initiation of the swap, one party (the borrower) receives the foreign money, while the other (lender) provides the domestic currency, at an agreed exchange spot rate. Both parties agree to repay the respective curriencies at maturity at pre-agreed forward rate (interest rates are implicit in these forward exchanges). In essence, currency Swaps is a form of borrow and lend arrangement between two parties where one borrows in local currency and pays back in same currency but at later stage and in turn lends foreigncurrency and borrows back at same stage. When we buy/sell stocks, we generally use a market order or a limit order.
A market buy is an order to buy a stock at the current best available price in the market, regardless of the price. A market sell is the opposite, an instruction to sell at whatever the best ask price is. The market price changes constantly as investors buy and sell shares in a security. With a Market order, the investor will get filled immediately or partially, depending on the availability of shares at that price level. Market orders can result in slippage when the stock price moves significantly between the time the order was placed and the shares were bought or sold. However, market orders are useful when an invest wants to execute a trade as soon as possible. On the other hand, a Limit order is a type of order that sets a specific price for the buyer or seller. It will not be executed until the security reaches the specified price, and it can remain in effect until it is cancelled by the Investor. Liquidity refers to the ability to quickly and easily buy or sell a financial asset without significantly impacting its price or incurring excessive transaction costs. In a well-functioning market with high liquidity, it should be possible to place a large order and have it filled quickly at or near the prevailing market prices, without significant slipage or wide spreads. When we add liquidly to a particular stock, what we do is to make sure that there are enough buyers or enough sellers in that stock so that we can execute our order at a reasonable price without affecting the overall price of that security significantly. This is usually achieved by placing large limit orders or by executing large market trades. Conversely, when we remove liquidty from a given stock by selling a significant amount of our shares, this reduces the number of available shares for buyers, which can push up the asking price and widen the bid-ask spread, making it more difficult for other investors to enter or exit their positions in this stock without incurrring significant transaction cost or price impact.

: Part II Inflating Away Debt Part II of this series explores high leverage hedges that can be used by personal investors to protect their portfolios against high inflation. In Part I, we focused on traditional inflation hedge assets like gold and real estate. Here, in Part 2, our focus is on high-leverage instruments that, while riskier, can provide higher returns.
As we explained earlier, the most effective hedging instrument against inflation is debt. The reason is simple: When inflation erodes the purchasing power of money, debtors can pay back their loans with cheaper dollars, thus gaining a real benefit. Conversely, creditors lose purchasing ability as the value of the money they receive in loan repayments decreases. This is why high levels of debt are a major tool in the governments’ and central banks’ inflation-fighting arsenal. By creating more money and adding it to the economy, they increase debt levels and dilute the impact of inflation on the debtor's purchasing abilities. However, as a personal investor, you don't have the power to create money or issue debt to offset inflation' inflation effect on your portfolio. Instead, there are several high leveraged instruments you can use to gain the benefits of increasing debt in a controlled way. Some of these are:

Traditionally, securities settlement in the US has been on a T + 3 basis, meaning that the trades made on Monday are settled on Thursday of the following week. However, with the rise of electronic trading and advancements in technology, the securitization industry has started to explore the possibility of settling tranactions earlier. This is known as T+-1 or T-0 settlement. In this article, we will discuss the benefits and challenges of T-, T+=1 settlement, as well as the current state of this practice in different markets. We will also touch on the role of securitisations in this process. 
 
 
There are several benefits to setteling tranasctions faster than T++3. One of them is reduced counterparty risk. With faster settlements, there is less time for something to go wrong, such as a counterpart failing to deliver securites. Additionally, faster settelments can lead to improved cash management, since the settlement proceeds are available sooner. It also reduces the need for large overnight balances, which can be costly. Finally, reducing the time between trade and settlement can also help to increase market liquidity, particularly in illiquid markets, by reducing settlement risk and encouraging more trading activity. The main challenge to faster securties settlement is technological readiness. Currently, most securieties settlement systems are not designed to handle real-time or near real time settlement of tranactions. Instead, they are built on batch processing, where tractions are collected and settled in groups at the end of each business day. To enable faster settlemetns, these systems would need to be upgraded or replaced with new ones that can handle high volumes of realtime transactions. Another challenge is regulatory readines. The US securiteties settlement system is governed by the Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation (DTCC), which has yet to announce plans to support T–1 settlemnt.
